readerTitle: Why IKEA hands you the screwdriver
caseNote: 실제 기업 (IKEA) + 회사가 전하는 일화 (다리를 뗀 테이블) + 가상 적용 (회계 사무소, 페인트 시공업체)
insight: 오래가는 원가 우위는 같은 일을 더 싸게 하는 데서가 아니라, 일을 없애거나 기꺼이 해 줄 사람에게 넘기도록 사업을 다시 설계하는 데서 나온다.
misconception: 원가 우위는 공급업체를 쥐어짜거나 싼 재료를 쓰는 데서 나온다.

sources.text: IKEA 공식 역사 자료 및 IKEA Museum (Älmhult): Gillis Lundgren과 플랫팩의 시작, 1950년대
IKEA, Democratic Design 소개 자료: 가격표를 먼저 정하고 디자인하는 방식
Porter, M. (1996). What Is Strategy? Harvard Business Review. (IKEA의 셀프서비스 모델, 매장 내 놀이방과 긴 영업시간)
IKEA Group press release, September 2017: TaskRabbit 인수

factChecks.note: 플랫팩 일화: IKEA는 직원 Gillis Lundgren이 1950년대 중반(자료에 따라 1956년) 테이블을 차에 싣기 위해 다리를 뗐다고 전합니다. 회사가 전하는 일화이므로 카드에 "the story IKEA tells"로 표시했습니다. 연도는 "mid-1950s"로만 적었습니다.
"가격표를 먼저 디자인한다"는 표현은 IKEA의 Democratic Design 자료와 여러 보도에 나옵니다. 게시 전 IKEA 공식 자료의 현재 문구를 확인하세요.
Porter(1996)가 IKEA 사례에서 셀프서비스, 고객의 직접 운반·조립, 매장 내 놀이방, 긴 영업시간을 언급하는지 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 레스토랑과 상세 가격표는 일반적으로 알려진 IKEA 매장 특징으로 적었습니다.
TaskRabbit 인수는 2017년 9월 발표 기준입니다. 인수 금액은 공개 자료마다 달라 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
회사 수치(매출, 점유율, 매장 수)는 일부러 쓰지 않았습니다. 넣을 경우 Ingka Group 연차 보고서로 확인하세요.

cards.title: The table that lost its legs
body: In the story IKEA tells about its early days, an employee named Gillis Lundgren couldn't fit a new table into a car. So he took the legs off.
It sounds like a moving-day trick. It became the core of one of the strongest cost advantages in retail.

image.label: A table with its legs removed, packed flat into a small car
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1950년대풍 작은 승용차 트렁크에 다리를 뗀 테이블 상판과 다리 네 개가 납작하게 쌓여 있음. 옆에 드라이버 하나. 실제 IKEA 로고, 노란·파란 브랜드 색 조합, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You want good furniture young families can afford.
body: You run a small furniture business in 1950s Sweden. Furniture is bulky, expensive to store and ship, and often damaged on the way. Your customers are young couples with little money.
How do you bring prices down?

options.text: Push your factories hard for lower prices
options.feedback: You save something, but every rival can bargain too. The bulky, costly steps between factory and living room stay the same.

options.text: Redesign the product and the store so customers pick, carry and build it
options.feedback: You remove whole steps instead of squeezing them. The price is that customers do more work, so the savings have to feel worth it.
Prices fall quickly, but so does quality. Customers notice when the shelf sags, and you've traded a cost problem for a reputation problem.

cards.title: Flat boxes changed everything around them.
body: IKEA designed furniture to ship in flat packs. Flat boxes take far less space on trucks and in warehouses, and they break less often.
Then it built stores around them. Customers browse a showroom, pull the boxes from a self-service warehouse, drive them home and assemble them.
Each step the customer does is a step IKEA doesn't pay staff, drivers or fitters to do. That saving shows up in the **price tag**.

cards.title: Follow one bookcase from shelf to living room.
body: At a traditional furniture store, staff or contractors handle most of these steps. At IKEA, the customer does.

breakdown.label: Browse
breakdown.detail: Tags and room displays replace a salesperson

breakdown.label: Pick
breakdown.detail: Pull the box from the warehouse shelf

breakdown.label: Deliver
breakdown.detail: A flat box fits in your own car

breakdown.label: Assemble
breakdown.detail: The final, costliest step moves to the buyer

cards.callout: Four jobs IKEA doesn't pay for, on every sale.
cards.softwareNote: Self-serve software works the same way. Customers sign up, set up and learn the product themselves through guides and templates, replacing sales calls and paid onboarding.

cards.title: Cost by design
body: **Cost by design** means building your cost advantage into how the work is done, not into how hard you bargain.
IKEA describes designing the price tag first. Developers start with a target price, then shape the product, materials and packaging to hit it.
The lasting savings came from steps that disappeared or moved to the customer. Paying suppliers less could only ever add a little.

image.label: A price tag drawn first, with a bookcase sketched around it
image.brief: 설계 도면 스타일 일러스트. 도면 한가운데 빈 가격표가 먼저 그려져 있고, 그 주변으로 책장의 선이 점점 그려지는 모습. 화살표로 "Price first → Design" 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Make the extra work easy to accept.
body: In his 1996 essay "What Is Strategy?", Michael Porter used IKEA as an example. It served young buyers willing to trade service for low prices.
IKEA also added things that make self-service bearable: a supervised play area for children, long opening hours, detailed tags and a restaurant for tired shoppers.
These cost money too. But they keep customers willing to do the work that saves far more.

cards.title: An accounting firm moves one step.
body: A small accounting firm spends hours each month chasing clients for receipts and retyping them.
It gives clients a simple upload page and a monthly checklist. Clients snap a photo of each receipt as it arrives. Staff stop chasing and start checking.
The firm can now offer a lower monthly fee than rivals and still earn more per client. The client does a small task they barely notice.

cards.title: Customers have to agree to the trade.
body: Not everyone wants to spend a Saturday building a wardrobe. In 2017, IKEA bought TaskRabbit, a service that connects people with local helpers for jobs like furniture assembly.
Moving work to customers only works when the lower price feels worth the effort, and when you make the work easy. Shift the work without lowering the price, and it just feels like bad service.

cards.title: Now you paint houses.
body: Your painting company competes with a cheaper rival. Your crews lose about a third of each job moving furniture, covering floors and clearing rooms before they can paint.
How do you lower your price without losing money?

options.text: Negotiate a bulk discount on paint
options.feedback: A real saving, but a small one, and your rival can get the same deal. The slow prep work is still on your bill.

options.text: Offer a cheaper "you prep" package with a clear checklist
options.feedback: Customers who want the lower price clear the rooms; your crew starts painting on arrival. You keep the full-service option for those who don't want the work.

options.text: Cut the price and push crews to work faster
options.feedback: Same work, less time. Quality slips, crews burn out, and your margin shrinks on every job.

cards.title: The cheapest step is the one you don't have to do.
body: IKEA's low prices come from a business designed to remove work or hand it to customers who accept the trade.
**Try it today:** list every step between your first contact with a customer and a finished job. Mark one you could remove, and one a customer might happily do for a lower price.
